For a fixed covered position \(i\), after the magician sees the \(N-2\) uncovered digits, his answer is a single ordered pair. Therefore that cover position can handle only one of the \(100\) possible hidden ordered pairs at that location.

Since the assistant has only \(N-1\) possible adjacent positions to cover, the \(100\) possible hidden pairs require
\[
N-1 \ge 100,
\]
so
\[
N \ge 101.
\]

Now show \(N=101\) works. Number the adjacent positions \(1,\dots,100\). Define coefficients
\[
c_j=
\begin{cases}
10,& j\text{ odd},\\
1,& j\text{ even}.
\end{cases}
\]
Let
\[
F(x_1,\dots,x_{101})=\sum_{j=1}^{101} c_j x_j \pmod{100}.
\]
The assistant covers the adjacent pair \(i,i+1\) where \(i\equiv F(x_1,\dots,x_{101}) \pmod{100}\), using \(0\) to mean position \(100\).

For any adjacent pair \(i,i+1\), the hidden digits \(a,b\) contribute either
\[
10a+b \quad \text{or} \quad a+10b,
\]
and both expressions determine the ordered pair \((a,b)\) uniquely. Thus, knowing the visible digits and \(i\), the magician can compute the unique hidden pair that makes \(F\) equal \(i\).

Therefore the smallest possible value is
\[
\boxed{101}.
\]
